newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU Parliament wants gene-altered corn sales ended.
newsitem.headline: EU Parliament wants gene-altered corn sales ended.

text.p: The European Parliament Tuesday demanded the suspension of all sales of genetically modified corn in the European Union, pending further health and safety tests.

Euro-MPs condemned the European Commission's market clearance of gene-altered U.S. corn, granted in the face of opposition from several EU governments, and accused the EU executive of not adequately analysing the long-term effects of genetic manipulations.
Parliament said the Commission acted irresponsibly last December when it authorised Ciba Geigy's Bt-corn even though a new EU food labelling law for such foods was not yet in effect.

The assembly warned Tuesday that imports of disease-resistant transgenic corn placed European producers in "an extremely disadvantageous competitive position" and would force them also to use GMO-based seed in spite of long-term risks of increasing resistance to pesticides and antibiotics.

During a debate on the controversy Monday night, Euro-MPs accused the Commission of making the same mistakes with genetically modified organisms as they had with mad cow disease, putting the interests of industry before those governing food safety and environmental protection.

European consumer concern about GMOs and food safety in general has grown since the continent's outbreak of mad cow disease, the fatal brain-wasting condition in cattle, and its perceived mishandling by Britain and the Commission.

European environment commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard said the Commission had fully consulted scientists before approving for EU release of products such as Ciba Geigy's insect-resistant corn and Monsanto Co.'s weedkiller-resistant soybeans.

But Euro-MPs protested that Austria and Luxembourg, which have slapped temporary national bans on transgenic corn imports, had come up with new evidence about the risks and the Commission should therefore suspend all sales until this data had been thoroughly examined.
Gene-altered corn can be imported into Europe but European farmers cannot yet grow it because it has not yet been added to the EU's list of new plant species.
In Vienna, Austrian environmentalists staged a protest outside the U.S. Embassy against the import of gene foods and sought inspiration from an unlikely source -- Elvis Presley.

As the Elvis hit "Return to Sender" blared out from a tape recorder, 30 activists from Greenpeace Austria ceremoniously dumped a ton of genetically altered soy outside the imposing entrance to the U.S. Embassy in central Vienna.
